questions.question: What is Spring Boot and why does it exist? It is an opinionated layer on Spring that auto-configures the framework, embeds a server, and removes boilerplate — so you can run a production-ready app with one command.
questions.title: Spring Boot Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that auto-configures the application based on classpath, embeds a web server (Tomcat/Jetty), and removes XML/boilerplate via sensible defaults — so a developer can run a production-ready application with `java -jar` or a single `main` method. It exists because the raw Spring Framework, while powerful, required significant manual configuration (XML, then Java config), dependency wiring, and an external servlet container to run; that ceremony slowed development and made onboarding hard. Spring Boot's auto-configuration, starters, and embedded server collapse weeks of plumbing into minutes, while staying 100% Spring under the hood.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Spring Boot as an opinionated auto-configuring layer on Spring (starters, embedded server, sensible defaults) rather than a different framework.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring Boot with Spring ('they're the same') — missing auto-configuration, starters, and the embedded server, which are the point of Boot; or believing Boot replaces Spring rather than configures it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame Boot as an opinionated layer ON Spring: auto-configuration (classpath-driven beans), starters (curated dependency sets), embedded server (run with one command), and sensible defaults over XML — while staying Spring underneath, so anything Spring can do, Boot can override.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that auto-configures the application based on the classpath, embeds a web server (Tomcat by default), and removes XML/boilerplate via sensible defaults — so a developer can run a production-ready application with `java -jar` or a single `main` method. It exists because the raw Spring Framework, while powerful, required significant manual configuration (XML, then Java config), explicit dependency wiring, and an external servlet container to deploy; that ceremony slowed development and made onboarding hard. Spring Boot's auto-configuration, starters, and embedded server collapse weeks of plumbing into minutes, while remaining 100% Spring under the hood — anything Spring can do, Boot can configure or override.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) auto-configuration — Boot inspects the classpath and creates beans you'd otherwise write (if Tomcat is present, it configures an embedded server; if a datasource is present, it configures one); (2) starters — curated, tested dependency sets (`spring-boot-starter-web` pulls Spring MVC + Tomcat + validation); (3) the embedded server — Tomcat/Jetty runs inside the jar, so the app is self-contained; (4) sensible defaults + externalized config — application.properties/yml overrides defaults; (5) the main method + `@SpringBootApplication` — combines config + component scan + auto-config; (6) production features — actuator (health/metrics), embedded server, executable jar; (7) it's still Spring — every Boot behavior is Spring beans you can override.

sections.title: Spring vs Spring Boot: What Each Adds
Auto-configuration, a starter, and the main method
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is convention versus control: Boot's auto-configuration gets you running in minutes but can make it unclear which beans exist and why ('magic'); the resolution is that every auto-config has a conditional and is overridable — you can always define your own bean to replace it, and actuator's /beans endpoint lists them. A second tension: starters make dependency sets easy but pull transitive deps you may not want, so understanding what a starter includes matters for slim builds. The third: the embedded server makes the app self-contained and 12-factor-friendly, but if you must deploy to an existing external container (legacy), Boot supports WAR packaging, trading some convenience for fit.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer ON Spring — auto-configuration, starters, embedded server, sensible defaults — not a different framework.
Auto-configuration inspects the classpath and creates beans you'd otherwise write (Tomcat, DataSource, MVC) — overridable by defining your own bean.
Starters are curated, tested dependency sets (spring-boot-starter-web) that prevent version conflicts.
The embedded server (Tomcat) runs inside the jar, so the app is self-contained and runnable with `java -jar`.
It's still Spring underneath — every Boot behavior is Spring beans; you can override any auto-config, and actuator lists them.
Externalized config (application.yml, env vars) overrides defaults; sensible defaults minimize boilerplate while keeping control available.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that auto-configures the application based on the classpath, embeds a web server, and removes XML and boilerplate via sensible defaults — so you can run a production-ready app with one command. It exists because raw Spring, while powerful, required significant manual configuration and an external servlet container to deploy, which slowed development and made onboarding hard. The pieces I anchor on are auto-configuration, which inspects the classpath and creates beans you'd otherwise write — if Tomcat's present it configures an embedded server, if a DataSource is present it configures one — and you override only what differs. Starters, which are curated, tested dependency sets that prevent version conflicts. The embedded server, which runs inside the jar so the app is self-contained and runnable with java -jar. And the fact that it's still Spring underneath — every Boot behavior is Spring beans, so I can override any auto-config by defining my own bean, and actuator's /beans endpoint lists what's there. The tension I'm honest about is convention versus control: the auto-configuration can feel like magic, but every auto-config has a conditional and is overridable, so the control is always there when I need it.

How does Spring Boot's auto-configuration decide which beans to create, and how do you override one?
What is a starter, and how does it prevent dependency version conflicts?
Why is the embedded server a 12-factor improvement over deploying a WAR to an external Tomcat?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Boot Fundamentals — Auto-configuration, Starters & Embedded Server
seo.metaDescription: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on Spring: auto-configuration, starters, embedded server, sensible defaults. Understand what Boot adds over Spring and how to override its magic.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work internally?
questions.title: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration — How It Works Internally
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configuration uses **`@EnableAutoConfiguration`** to scan `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (or `spring.factories` in pre-2.7) for candidate configuration classes. Each candidate is conditionally applied using **`@ConditionalOn*` annotations** that check for the presence of classes, beans, or properties. This lets Spring Boot configure sensible defaults without requiring explicit XML or Java configuration. **There is no scanning, no guessing** — every auto-configuration class is a regular `@Configuration` guarded by conditions; activation is deterministic given the same classpath, properties, and user-defined beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the mechanism behind Spring Boot's 'magic' rather than just using it as a black box
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'Spring Boot just auto-configures things' without explaining how conditions and the imports file drive the process
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the difference between `spring.factories` (pre-2.7) and `AutoConfiguration.imports` (2.7+), and how `@AutoConfigureAfter`/`@AutoConfigureBefore` control ordering

sections.title: Auto-Configuration Isn't Magic — It's a Pipeline of Conditional @Configuration Classes
sections.content:
Most developers describe Spring Boot auto-configuration as 'it just figures out what you need.
- That's the experience, not the mechanism.
- Under the hood, auto-configuration is a **deterministic pipeline**: Boot discovers a list of candidate `@Configuration` classes from a well-known file on the classpath, evaluates a set of `@Conditional` annotations on each one, and only registers the beans from classes whose conditions all pass.

**There is no scanning, no guessing, no AI.** Every auto-configuration class is a regular `@Configuration` class with `@Bean` methods — the same kind you'd write yourself. The only difference is that each one is guarded by conditions like `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, and `@ConditionalOnProperty`.

When you add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` to your POM, Boot doesn't 'detect' that you want JPA — it finds `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` in its imports file, checks that `javax.sql.DataSource` is on the classpath, confirms you haven't defined your own, and wires one with HikariCP defaults. **Same classpath, same properties, same user beans = same context, every time**.

sections.title: Auto-Configuration Pipeline — From @EnableAutoConfiguration to Wired Beans
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    BootApp["@SpringBootApplication"]
    EnableAuto["@EnableAutoConfiguration"]
    Selector["AutoConfigurationImportSelector"]
    Imports["AutoConfiguration.imports file"]
    Candidates["~150 candidate auto-config classes"]
    ClassCheck{"@ConditionalOnClass"}
    PropCheck{"@ConditionalOnProperty"}
    BeanCheck{"@ConditionalOnMissingBean"}
    OrderApply["Apply @AutoConfigureBefore / After"]
    BeanReg["Register beans into ApplicationContext"]
    Skipped["Skipped (negative match)"]
    Report["Conditions Evaluation Report"]

    BootApp --> EnableAuto
    EnableAuto --> Selector
    Selector --> Imports
    Imports --> Candidates
    Candidates --> ClassCheck
    ClassCheck -->|present| PropCheck
    ClassCheck -->|absent| Skipped
    PropCheck -->|matches| BeanCheck
    PropCheck -->|no match| Skipped
    BeanCheck -->|user bean absent| OrderApply
    BeanCheck -->|user bean present| Skipped
    OrderApply --> BeanReg
    BeanReg --> Report
    Skipped --> Report
```

sections.title: Phase 1 — Discovery: How Boot Finds 150+ Candidate Configuration Classes
sections.content:
**The trigger**
- `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration` imports `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`
- The selector reads a file that lists every auto-configuration class Boot ships

**The imports file**
- Spring Boot 2.7+: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
- Pre-2.7: `META-INF/spring.factories` under the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key
- One fully-qualified class name per line in the new format
- Boot 3.x ships ~150 candidate classes

**Why the format change**
- `spring.factories` was overloaded — handled auto-configuration, listeners, initializers, failure analyzers all in one file
- The dedicated imports file is faster to parse and makes auto-config candidates obvious
- Both formats still work in Boot 3.x for backward compatibility

**Discovery is exhaustive — filtering is selective**
- All ~150 candidates are loaded as candidates
- Loading the class doesn't mean its beans get registered
- Condition evaluation in the next phase decides what activates

sections.title: Phase 2 — Condition Evaluation: The @ConditionalOn* Chain That Decides Everything
sections.content:
**Evaluation order — cheap checks first**
- `@ConditionalOnClass` evaluated first; cheapest filter
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` next; reads the `Environment`
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` last; requires partial bean inspection

**The most common conditions**
- `@ConditionalOnClass(SomeLib.class)` — checks classpath without loading; if absent, the auto-config is skipped before any bean definitions are read
- `@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "...", havingValue = "...", matchIfMissing = true)` — toggles activation by property; supports opt-out by default
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` — backs off when the user defined their own bean; the foundation of override-friendliness
- `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` / `@ConditionalOnNotWebApplication` — servlet vs reactive vs CLI
- `@ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class)` — depends on another bean already in the context

**Why `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` matters most**
- It's the mechanism behind 'convention over configuration'
- Boot provides the default; your explicit bean overrides it silently
- Without it, the user gets `BeanDefinitionOverrideException` on customization

**Tracing what happened**

```properties
logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=conditions
```

- Run with `--debug` or hit `/actuator/conditions`
- Three sections: positive matches (applied), negative matches (skipped + reason), exclusions
- The single most useful tool for debugging auto-config issues

sections.title: Phase 3 — Ordering and Exclusion
sections.content:
**Ordering with @AutoConfigureAfter / @AutoConfigureBefore**
- Auto-configuration classes don't run in random order
- Declare dependencies on each other explicitly
- `JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration` declares `@AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` because JPA needs a DataSource

**Why ordering matters**
- Getting it wrong in a custom auto-config is a common source of `BeanCreationException` at startup
- If your auto-config creates a bean that depends on another auto-configured bean, declare the ordering explicitly
- Spring won't infer it from the bean dependency graph at the auto-configuration level

**Excluding an auto-configuration entirely**

```java
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class })
public class App { }
```

```yaml
spring.autoconfigure.exclude: org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
```

- Cleaner than fighting conditions with dummy beans
- Type-safe at the annotation site (Java) vs string-based (property)
- Useful when a starter pulls in something you don't want

**Determinism guarantee**
- Same classpath + same properties + same user beans → same `ApplicationContext`, every time
- When something changes, `/actuator/conditions` shows exactly which condition flipped

sections.title: Auto-Configuration Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When auto-configuration helps:**
- Greenfield apps where defaults match the desired setup
- Reusable starters that consumers can drop in without manual wiring
- Standardizing baseline configuration (logging, metrics, security) across many services

**When auto-configuration hurts:**
- Specialized configurations where defaults conflict with custom setup
- Multi-DataSource scenarios where Boot's single-DataSource auto-config gets in the way
- Debugging unexpected bean wiring without consulting `/actuator/conditions`

**Watch for:**
- Multiple starters defining beans of the same type — `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` decides which wins
- Auto-config classes activated unintentionally via transitive dependencies — exclude explicitly
- Conditional evaluation cost at startup — Boot 3 AOT can pre-evaluate conditions for native images
- Ordering cycles between custom auto-configs — Spring detects and throws `IllegalStateException` at startup
- `@Configuration` instead of `@AutoConfiguration` for custom auto-configs — loses ordering guarantees

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@EnableAutoConfiguration` loads candidate classes from `AutoConfiguration.imports`** — Spring Boot 2.7+ uses `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`; pre-2.7 used `META-INF/spring.factories`.
- **Every auto-config class is `@Conditional` — never truly unconditional** — `@ConditionalOnClass` checks the classpath; `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` checks the registry; user-defined beans always take precedence.
- **Auto-configuration runs after user configuration** — `@Configuration` classes from your packages are processed first; auto-config is effectively the fallback.
- **`--debug` prints the Conditions Evaluation Report** — three sections: positive (matched and applied), negative (checked and skipped), exclusions; the only reliable way to know why an auto-config fired or did not.
- **`spring.autoconfigure.exclude` removes a class entirely** — prevents an auto-config from being evaluated even if its conditions would match; useful when a starter pulls in something you do not want.
- **`@AutoConfigureAfter` / `@AutoConfigureBefore` for ordering** — declare dependencies between auto-configs explicitly; Spring won't infer ordering from bean dependencies.
- **Discovery is exhaustive; filtering is selective** — all ~150 candidates load, then conditions decide which register beans.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When Spring Boot 'just works' without any configuration, auto-configuration is what is happening behind the scenes. It is not magic — it is conditional bean registration driven by what is on your classpath and what beans you have already defined.

**How it is discovered**
- `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which reads `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Spring Boot 2.7+) listing hundreds of candidate auto-configuration classes
- Each class is evaluated for its `@Conditional` annotations before any beans are created

**How conditions decide what registers**
- `@ConditionalOnClass(HikariDataSource.class)` — only apply this config if HikariCP is on the classpath
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` — only apply if you have not already defined a `DataSource`; this is how your custom bean overrides the default
- Your `@Configuration` classes are processed before auto-configuration — auto-config is always the fallback, never the override

**Ordering**
- `@AutoConfigureAfter` / `@AutoConfigureBefore` declare dependencies between auto-configurations
- Without explicit ordering, beans depending on auto-configured collaborators may fail at startup

**Debugging**
- Add `--debug` to the JVM arguments and Spring prints the Conditions Evaluation Report at startup
- Three sections: positive matches (auto-config that ran), negative matches (auto-config that was skipped and why), and exclusions
- `spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration` removes a class entirely when a starter pulls in something unwanted

In an interview, the strong answer is: **auto-configuration is a deterministic pipeline of conditional `@Configuration` classes discovered from a registration file; the same inputs always produce the same context**.

questions.question: What are the key phases of the Spring Boot startup sequence when SpringApplication.run() is called?
questions.title: Spring Boot Startup Sequence (SpringApplication.run Phases)
questions.direct_answer: `SpringApplication.run()` orchestrates a multi-phase startup: it **prepares the environment**, **creates and refreshes the `ApplicationContext`**, then **calls runners** and **publishes a final `ApplicationReadyEvent`**. Each phase is observable via `SpringApplicationRunListeners` and typed `ApplicationEvent`s. The order matters for your custom logic: `@PostConstruct` runs during bean initialization inside refresh; `CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` run after refresh and the embedded server has bound its port; `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires when the app is ready to accept traffic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can trace the lifecycle beyond 'the context starts' and explain where things like property loading and bean initialization happen
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing `ApplicationRunner`/`CommandLineRunner` (called after context is ready) with `@PostConstruct` (called during bean initialization inside context refresh)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `SpringApplicationRunListeners` and the exact `ApplicationEvent` types (`ApplicationStartingEvent`, `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent`, etc.) and where to hook custom logic safely

sections.title: Why Knowing the Startup Sequence Matters More Than Memorizing Event Names
sections.content:
Most developers think of `SpringApplication.run()` as 'it starts the app.
- But this single method orchestrates a multi-phase lifecycle where **the order of operations determines where your custom logic can safely run**.
- The most common bug from misunderstanding this sequence is putting initialization code in `@PostConstruct` that depends on the full application context being ready — it isn't. `@PostConstruct` runs during bean initialization inside context refresh, before runners, before the server port is bound, and before `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires.

The startup sequence is observable through `SpringApplicationRunListeners`, which broadcast typed events at each phase boundary. These aren't just debugging aids — they're the **hook points** where you can inject custom behavior: registering metrics before the context exists, modifying the environment before property binding, or running migration scripts after the context is fully wired but before the app accepts traffic.

Understanding the sequence also explains why startup is slow. Each phase has a measurable cost, and Spring Boot 3.x added startup tracking via `ApplicationStartup` to let you pinpoint exactly which phase is consuming time.

sections.title: Spring Boot Startup Sequence
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Main
    participant SpringApp as SpringApplication
    participant Listeners as RunListeners
    participant Env as Environment
    participant Ctx as ApplicationContext
    participant Server as Embedded Server

    Main->>SpringApp: run(App.class, args)
    SpringApp->>Listeners: ApplicationStartingEvent
    SpringApp->>Env: prepareEnvironment
    Env->>Listeners: ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent
    SpringApp->>Ctx: createApplicationContext
    Ctx->>Listeners: ApplicationContextInitializedEvent
    SpringApp->>Ctx: load bean definitions
    Ctx->>Listeners: ApplicationPreparedEvent
    SpringApp->>Ctx: refresh
    Ctx->>Ctx: instantiate beans, inject deps, run PostConstruct
    Ctx->>Server: start embedded server, bind port
    SpringApp->>Listeners: ApplicationStartedEvent
    SpringApp->>Ctx: callRunners (CommandLineRunner, ApplicationRunner)
    SpringApp->>Listeners: ApplicationReadyEvent
```

sections.title: Phase 1 — Environment Preparation and Context Creation
sections.content:
**Bootstrap and listeners**
- `SpringApplication.run()` creates a `DefaultBootstrapContext`
- `SpringApplicationRunListeners` notified with `ApplicationStartingEvent`
- No beans, no properties, no `ApplicationContext` exists yet
- This is where logging framework initialization happens

**Environment preparation**
- Spring builds the `Environment` by layering property sources in precedence order
- System properties override `application.yml`, which overrides `application.properties`, which overrides defaults
- `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent` fires here
- The last safe point to programmatically add or modify property sources before anything reads them
- The hook for vault secret injection (Spring Cloud Vault uses this)

**Context creation**
- Spring picks the context type based on the classpath
- `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext` for servlet web apps
- `AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContext` for WebFlux
- `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` for non-web
- `ApplicationContextInitializedEvent` fires after creation but before refresh

**Failure surface**
- Exception before refresh produces `ApplicationFailedEvent` and the JVM exits
- Exception in a runner aborts startup *after* the server bound the port
- Exception after `ApplicationReadyEvent` is just a normal runtime error

sections.title: Phase 2 — Context Refresh: Bean Instantiation and @PostConstruct
sections.content:
**Where most startup time is spent**
- `ApplicationPreparedEvent` fires just before refresh begins
- The context exists, the main configuration class is registered, but no beans are instantiated

**Refresh sequence**
- Spring processes all `@Configuration` classes (including auto-configurations filtered by `@Conditional` annotations)
- Creates bean definitions, then instantiates singletons
- Dependency injection wires collaborators
- `@PostConstruct` methods run during individual bean initialization
- `BeanPostProcessor`s wrap beans (e.g., AOP proxies for `@Transactional`)

**A common @PostConstruct mistake**
- Assuming `@PostConstruct` has access to the complete application context
- Other singletons may not have been created yet — initialization order is unpredictable for parallel branches
- The web server hasn't started; the port isn't bound
- Use a runner instead when you need 'all beans ready and server bound'

**Embedded server startup**
- For web applications, refresh creates and starts the embedded server
- The server binds to its port during refresh
- A port conflict causes `ApplicationContext` refresh failure, not a separate error

**Context refreshed**
- `ContextRefreshedEvent` fires when refresh completes
- All singleton beans are instantiated, all `@PostConstruct` methods have run, the server is listening
- But the application is not yet considered 'started' — that's the next phase

sections.title: Phase 3 — Runners and Ready: The Safe Zone for Application-Level Initialization
Hook Selection Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When `@PostConstruct` helps:**
- Per-bean initialization that depends only on injected collaborators
- Validating constructor-injected configuration
- Building per-bean caches

**When `@PostConstruct` hurts:**
- Logic that depends on every bean being ready — order is unpredictable
- Anything needing the embedded server bound
- Cross-bean coordination — use a runner or `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)`

**When runners help:**
- One-time data seeding, migration validation, or external service ping checks
- Logic that should run after `@PostConstruct` but before traffic
- Multiple ordered initialization steps via `@Order`

**Watch for:**
- Long-running runners delaying `ApplicationReadyEvent` and the readiness probe
- Runners that depend on external services that might be down at startup — fail fast or retry?
- Confusing `ApplicationStartedEvent` with `ApplicationReadyEvent` — runners haven't run at the former
- `SpringApplicationRunListeners` registered via `spring.factories` for early events vs `@EventListener` beans for post-context events

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PostConstruct` fires before runners; runners fire after the context is fully ready** — the order is: instantiate beans → inject → `@PostConstruct` → `ApplicationStartedEvent` → runners → `ApplicationReadyEvent`.
- **`CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` execute after all beans are created** — safe to call any injected service; `@PostConstruct` is not safe for logic that depends on the full context being operational.
- **Multiple runners use `@Order` or `Ordered`** — lower value = higher priority; unordered runners execute in registration order.
- **`SpringApplicationRunListeners` vs `ApplicationListener`** — `SpringApplicationRunListeners` fire before the `ApplicationContext` is created (too early for `@Bean`); `ApplicationListener` or `@EventListener` fires after.
- **`ApplicationFailedEvent` fires if startup fails** — use it to emit metrics or alerts before the JVM exits; not fired on graceful shutdown, only on exception during startup.
- **Embedded server binds during refresh** — port conflicts surface as `ApplicationContext` refresh failures, not separate errors.
- **`ApplicationReadyEvent` is the readiness probe contract** — Kubernetes should not route traffic before this fires.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot's startup follows a precise sequence that determines when each hook is safe to use. Getting the order wrong means initialization code runs before its dependencies are ready.

**The sequence**
- `ApplicationStartingEvent` → environment prep → `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent` → context creation → bean definition load → `ApplicationPreparedEvent` → refresh
- During refresh: bean instantiation, dependency injection, `@PostConstruct`, `BeanPostProcessor`s, embedded server start
- `ApplicationStartedEvent` fires after refresh
- Runners (`CommandLineRunner`, `ApplicationRunner`) execute next
- `ApplicationReadyEvent` marks the application as ready for traffic

**What goes where**
- `@PostConstruct`: initialization that depends only on injected collaborators — cache warmup, connection validation
- Runners: startup logic that should run after the full context is ready — data seeding, integration checks, feature flag registration
- `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)`: same timing as runners but declared as an event listener rather than implementing an interface
- `EnvironmentPostProcessor`: add property sources from external systems (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) before any bean reads the environment

**Multiple runners**
- Execute in `@Order` sequence — lower value runs first
- `CommandLineRunner` receives raw `String[] args`; `ApplicationRunner` receives a typed `ApplicationArguments` object — the only practical difference

**Failure semantics**
- Exception during refresh → `ApplicationFailedEvent` and JVM exits
- Exception in a runner → `ApplicationFailedEvent`; server already bound the port (load balancer briefly sees an open port that immediately closes)

In an interview, the strong answer is: **`@PostConstruct` for per-bean init, runners or `ApplicationReadyEvent` for context-wide init, `EnvironmentPostProcessor` for early property injection — pick the hook by what state must already exist when it fires**.

questions.question: What does @SpringBootApplication do and what three annotations does it combine?
questions.title: @SpringBootApplication — What It Combines
questions.direct_answer: `@SpringBootApplication` is a convenience meta-annotation that combines **`@SpringBootConfiguration`** (a specialised `@Configuration` enforced as singleton per context), **`@EnableAutoConfiguration`** (triggers auto-configuration scanning), and **`@ComponentScan`** (scans the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages for Spring components). The component scan boundary is the **package containing the annotated class** — sibling packages are invisible. Use `scanBasePackageClasses` for refactoring-safe explicit scan paths and `exclude = {...}` to prevent unwanted auto-configurations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands component scanning scope and can explain why placing the main class in the root package matters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing the main class inside a sub-package so that sibling packages are missed by `@ComponentScan`, causing beans not to be found
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you can narrow or widen the scan with `scanBasePackages`/`scanBasePackageClasses`, and that `@SpringBootConfiguration` differs from `@Configuration` because only one is allowed per application context

sections.title: Three Annotations in a Trenchcoat — and Package Placement Is the Hidden Gotcha
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a meta-annotation that combines three annotations into one. Knowing the three names is the easy part — understanding **what each one actually triggers and the subtle constraint that catches most teams** is what interviewers are really testing.

The three annotations are **`@SpringBootConfiguration`** (a specialized `@Configuration` that marks this class as the application's primary configuration source), **`@EnableAutoConfiguration`** (triggers the auto-configuration pipeline that scans `AutoConfiguration.imports` for conditional configuration classes), and **`@ComponentScan`** (scans the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages for `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` beans).

The critical detail is `@ComponentScan`'s default behavior.
- It scans **from the package of the annotated class downward**.
- If your main class lives in `com.example.app.config` and your controllers are in `com.example.app.web`, both get scanned.
- But if your main class is in `com.example.app.config` and your service is in `com.example.service`, **that service package is a sibling, not a child — it will never be found**.
- This is the most common reason for 'bean not found' errors in new Spring Boot projects.

sections.title: What Each Annotation Controls
sections.content:
**`@SpringBootConfiguration`**
- A specialized `@Configuration`
- Spring Boot enforces that **only one** `@SpringBootConfiguration` exists per application context
- Prevents accidental duplicate context creation in tests
- `@SpringBootTest` walks up the package hierarchy looking for exactly one — two would cause an ambiguous configuration error

**`@EnableAutoConfiguration`**
- The trigger for Boot's auto-configuration pipeline
- Selectively disable auto-configurations using the `exclude` attribute
- Type-safe and visible at the annotation site

```java
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {
    DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class,
    HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration.class
})
public class App { }
```

**`@ComponentScan`**
- The one you'll customize most
- Defaults to scanning the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages
- `scanBasePackages` (string-based) or `scanBasePackageClasses` (type-safe) explicitly declare scan roots

**Refactoring-safe scan configuration**

```java
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackageClasses = {
    CoreMarker.class,
    WebMarker.class
})
public class App { }
```

- `CoreMarker` and `WebMarker` are placeholder interfaces in the packages you want scanned
- Renaming the package fails at compile time — strings would silently break

sections.title: When to Override Scan Defaults — Multi-Module Projects and the Test Discovery Rule
sections.content:
**Single-module convention**
- Place the main class in the root package (e.g., `com.example.app`)
- Let `@ComponentScan` discover everything beneath it
- Path of least resistance; any deviation requires explicit configuration

**Multi-module project pattern**
- `core` module at `com.example.core`; `web` module at `com.example.web`
- If the main class lives in `com.example.web`, beans from `com.example.core` are in a sibling package — not scanned
- Fix 1: `scanBasePackages = {"com.example"}` (scan the shared parent)
- Fix 2: `@Import(CoreConfiguration.class)` (explicit import; more surgical)

**The test discovery rule**
- `@SpringBootTest` walks up the package tree from the test class to find the nearest `@SpringBootConfiguration`
- If the test is in `com.example.web.controller` and the main class is in `com.example.web`, it's found correctly
- If the main class is in a different hierarchy, `@SpringBootTest` fails with `Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration`
- Safest: keep test classes in the same root or use `@SpringBootTest(classes = Application.class)`

**`scanBasePackageClasses` is strictly better than `scanBasePackages`**
- Marker class reference fails at compile time when the package is renamed
- String-based references silently become wrong with no startup error
- Pay the small cost of creating an empty interface per package; gain refactoring safety

**Excluding beans from scan**

```java
@SpringBootApplication
@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(
    type = FilterType.ASSIGNABLE_TYPE,
    classes = LegacyService.class
))
public class App { }
```

sections.title: @SpringBootApplication Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When the meta-annotation helps:**
- Standard single-module application with the main class at the root package
- Clear convention; new team members understand it immediately
- One annotation instead of three on the entry point

**When the meta-annotation hurts:**
- Multi-module projects where the scan boundary doesn't match package layout
- Library code that needs `@Configuration` without auto-configuration triggering
- Tests that need only part of the behavior — decompose into the three constituent annotations

**Watch for:**
- Main class buried in a sub-package — sibling packages are invisible
- Two `@SpringBootConfiguration` classes — ambiguous configuration error in `@SpringBootTest`
- `scanBasePackages` strings that go stale after a package rename — use `scanBasePackageClasses`
- Forgetting `exclude` and getting database auto-config in a CLI app — wastes startup time
- Putting `@SpringBootApplication` on a non-entry-point class — works but confuses readers

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootApplication` = `@SpringBootConfiguration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`** — decompose it when you only need part of the behavior.
- **Main class package determines the default scan boundary** — classes in `com.example.common` are invisible if the main class is in `com.example.app`; move the main class to the root package or use `scanBasePackages`.
- **`scanBasePackageClasses` is refactoring-safe; `scanBasePackages` (strings) is not** — renaming a package breaks the string reference silently; referencing a marker class fails at compile time.
- **`exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}` prevents unwanted auto-config** — cleaner than `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property because it is type-safe and visible at the annotation site.
- **Do not place `@SpringBootApplication` inside a sub-package** — the scan covers the annotated class's package and all sub-packages; a main class in `com.example.app.main` will not scan `com.example.app.service` if it is a sibling, not a descendant.
- **`@SpringBootConfiguration` is enforced as singleton per context** — `@SpringBootTest` finds exactly one or fails with ambiguous configuration.
- **`@SpringBootTest(classes = App.class)` bypasses auto-discovery** — useful when test class hierarchy doesn't align with main class package.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a single annotation that composes three: `@SpringBootConfiguration` (this class is a primary bean source enforced as singleton per context), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (activate Spring Boot's auto-configuration), and `@ComponentScan` (scan from this class's package downward).

**The scan boundary rule**
- The component scan starts from the package containing the `@SpringBootApplication` class
- Place the main class in the root package (`com.example`) so every sub-package (`com.example.service`, `com.example.repository`) is automatically discovered
- A main class buried inside a sub-package means sibling packages are outside the scan boundary — beans there are invisible

**Customizing the scan**
- `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "com.example")` extends the boundary, but string-based — renaming the package breaks it silently
- `scanBasePackageClasses = {ServiceMarker.class}` is refactoring-safe — a compile error tells you immediately when the marker class moves

**Excluding auto-configurations**
- `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class})` prevents that auto-config from running — useful when a starter pulls in database config you do not want
- Type-safe and visible at the annotation site; prefer this over the string-based property approach

**Test discovery**
- `@SpringBootTest` walks up from the test class to find one `@SpringBootConfiguration`
- Two configurations cause ambiguous configuration errors
- `@SpringBootTest(classes = App.class)` bypasses auto-discovery when class hierarchies don't align

In an interview, the strong answer is: **the three annotations are easy; the test is whether you understand the scan boundary, the singleton constraint, and refactoring-safe scan configuration**.

questions.question: How do you write and register a custom Spring Boot auto-configuration?
questions.title: Custom Auto-Configuration (spring.factories / AutoConfiguration.imports)
questions.direct_answer: Create an **`@AutoConfiguration` class** with `@ConditionalOn*` guards, implement your `@Bean` methods, then register the class in **`META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`** (Spring Boot 2.7+) so Spring Boot discovers it at startup. Use the **two-module starter pattern** — an `autoconfigure` module containing the `@AutoConfiguration` class plus a thin `starter` POM that aggregates dependencies. Always annotate `@Bean` methods with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` so consumers can override defaults. Test with `ApplicationContextRunner` for fast assertions on bean presence and override behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the registration mechanism and knows how to write safe conditions so the auto-configuration backs off correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to add the registration file (the `@AutoConfiguration` class is never discovered), or using `@Configuration` instead of `@AutoConfiguration` which bypasses ordering guarantees
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the full starter module layout (autoconfigure JAR + starter POM), explain how `@AutoConfigureAfter`/`@AutoConfigureBefore` work, and show how `spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates IDE metadata from `@ConfigurationProperties`

sections.title: The Registration File Most Developers Forget — and Why Their Auto-Configuration Silently Does Nothing
sections.content:
The number one mistake when writing custom auto-configuration is forgetting the registration file.
- You create a perfectly valid `@AutoConfiguration` class with all the right conditions, but Spring Boot never discovers it because **auto-configuration classes are not found by component scanning**.
- They must be explicitly listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Boot 2.7+) or `META-INF/spring.factories` (pre-2.7).

This is intentional. Auto-configuration classes live in shared libraries — JARs consumed by other applications. Component scanning would only find them if the consumer happened to scan the right package, making the behavior dependent on the consumer's package structure. The registration file makes discovery **explicit and package-independent**.

The standard pattern for production library auto-configuration is a **two-module layout**: an `autoconfigure` module containing the `@AutoConfiguration` class, its `@ConfigurationProperties` POJO, and the registration file; and a `starter` module that depends on the autoconfigure module plus all required transitive dependencies.
- **The starter POM has no Java code** — it's a dependency aggregator.
- Spring's own starters follow this exact pattern.

sections.title: Writing the @AutoConfiguration Class
The Two-Module Starter Layout
sections.content:
**Module structure**

```
metrics-parent (pom)
metrics-spring-boot-autoconfigure
  src/main/java/com/example/metrics/
    MetricsAutoConfiguration.java
    MetricsProperties.java
    MetricsService.java
  src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/
    org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
metrics-spring-boot-starter
  pom.xml (depends on metrics-spring-boot-autoconfigure)
```

**The registration file**

```
com.example.metrics.MetricsAutoConfiguration
```

- One fully-qualified class name per line
- No comments, no blank lines at the end
- Lives at `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`

**The starter POM is empty**

```xml
<artifactId>metrics-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.example</groupId>
        <artifactId>metrics-spring-boot-autoconfigure</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

**`@ConfigurationProperties` (record-based)**

```java
@ConfigurationProperties("metrics")
public record MetricsProperties(String endpoint, Duration interval) {
    public MetricsProperties {
        endpoint = endpoint != null ? endpoint : "http://localhost:9090";
        interval = interval != null ? interval : Duration.ofSeconds(30);
    }
}
```

**Why two modules**
- Consumers add only the starter — get all transitive dependencies
- Advanced consumers can depend on `autoconfigure` directly, bypassing transitive deps
- Mirrors how Spring's own starters are structured

sections.title: Testing with ApplicationContextRunner and IDE Metadata
Custom Auto-Configuration Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When custom auto-configuration helps:**
- Reusable libraries with optional Spring integration
- Internal platform starters that bundle observability, security, logging baselines
- Standardizing configuration across many services

**When custom auto-configuration hurts:**
- One-off configuration shared between two services in the same repo — `@Import` is lighter
- Libraries with significant logic that consumers always customize — provide a `Customizer<T>` interface instead
- Teams unfamiliar with `/actuator/conditions` debugging

**Watch for:**
- Forgetting the registration file — silent no-op
- `@Configuration` instead of `@AutoConfiguration` — loses ordering machinery
- Missing `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — consumer can't override; reports as 'duplicate bean' instead of 'override applied'
- Business classes inside the starter JAR — should live in autoconfigure or a core lib
- Forcing dependency versions that conflict with the Boot BOM — consumers can't override
- Skipping the negative-case test (`FilteredClassLoader`) — silent NoClassDefFoundError in consumer apps

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Auto-configuration class must be registered to be discovered** — Spring Boot 2.7+: list in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`; pre-2.7: list in `META-INF/spring.factories` under `EnableAutoConfiguration`.
- **Starter layout: two modules** — `my-feature-autoconfigure` (contains `@AutoConfiguration` + `@Conditional` logic); `my-feature-spring-boot-starter` (POM-only, depends on autoconfigure + feature library).
- **User beans always win — put `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on every auto-configured bean** — this lets users override any default by defining their own bean of that type.
- **`@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` controls ordering** — if your auto-config depends on a `DataSource` bean existing first, declare the dependency explicitly.
- **Test auto-configuration with `ApplicationContextRunner`** — creates a minimal application context without starting Spring Boot; assert which beans are registered, override behavior, and negative cases.
- **Always test the negative case** — use `FilteredClassLoader` to simulate the class not being on the classpath; proves `@ConditionalOnClass` is wired correctly.
- **`spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates IDE metadata** — consumer IDEs auto-complete your custom properties without warnings.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Writing a custom auto-configuration is how you package reusable Spring Boot behavior into a library that others use by simply adding the dependency — no manual bean registration required.

**The registration file**
- Spring Boot 2.7+: create `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` listing the fully-qualified class name of your `@AutoConfiguration` class
- Without this file, Spring Boot never discovers your class — the most common mistake when writing the first custom auto-configuration

**Starter module layout**
- `my-feature-autoconfigure` JAR: contains the `@AutoConfiguration` class with `@Conditional` logic and bean definitions
- `my-feature-spring-boot-starter` POM: depends on `autoconfigure` + the feature library; users add only the starter dependency and get everything

**The override contract**
- Every auto-configured bean must have `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — if the user defines their own bean of that type, yours is skipped
- Use `@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` when your beans depend on a `DataSource` being available

**Testing**
- `ApplicationContextRunner` is the standard testing tool — creates a minimal context, applies your auto-configuration, and lets you assert which beans registered
- Three tests every auto-config needs: defaults, user override, negative case (`FilteredClassLoader`)
- No need to start the full application; tests run in milliseconds

**IDE metadata**
- Add `spring-boot-configuration-processor` as `optional`
- Generates `spring-configuration-metadata.json` so consumer IDEs auto-complete `myprefix.*` properties

In an interview, the strong answer is: **two modules, `@AutoConfiguration` + `@ConditionalOnClass` + `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, registration file, three tests including the negative case, and the configuration processor for IDE support**.

questions.question: How do you customize Spring Boot startup — banners, listeners, and FailureAnalyzer?
questions.title: Customizing Spring Boot Startup — Banner, Listeners, and FailureAnalyzer
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot's startup is customizable at three levels: the **banner** (visual branding via `banner.txt` or a `Banner` bean), **application listeners** (reacting to lifecycle events before the context exists, registered via `spring.factories`), and **`FailureAnalyzer`** (converting cryptic startup exceptions into human-readable messages with fix suggestions). `FailureAnalyzer` is the most production-relevant — it turns a 200-line stack trace into a clear message like 'Port 8080 is already in use' with an actionable next step. Use `EnvironmentPostProcessor` for early property injection (vault secrets) before any bean reads the `Environment`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows about startup hooks beyond basic configuration and can explain `FailureAnalyzer`
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing `ApplicationListener` with `@EventListener` — `ApplicationListener` registered via `spring.factories` works before the context exists; `@EventListener` requires a bean and only works after context creation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain writing a custom `FailureAnalyzer` to provide team-specific error messages for common deployment issues like missing environment variables

sections.title: Three Startup Hooks Most Developers Never Use
sections.content:
Most Spring Boot developers know `application.yml` and `@SpringBootApplication`. But the startup sequence has three customization points that solve real problems: **banner customization** for identifying which version is running in logs, **application listeners** for reacting to lifecycle events before the `ApplicationContext` exists, and **`FailureAnalyzer`** for turning cryptic startup exceptions into human-readable messages.

Of these three, **`FailureAnalyzer` is the most production-relevant but least known**.
- When Spring Boot fails to start, the default behavior is a 200-line stack trace that buries the actual cause. `FailureAnalyzer`s intercept specific exceptions and produce clear messages like 'Port 8080 is already in use' with a suggested action.
- **You can write custom `FailureAnalyzer`s** for your team's common deployment issues — missing environment variables, incompatible database schemas, unreachable configuration servers.

The key distinction with listeners is that **`ApplicationListener` registered via `spring.factories` works before the `ApplicationContext` exists** — unlike `@EventListener`, which requires a bean in the context. This makes listeners the only way to react to early startup events like `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent`.

sections.title: Writing a Custom FailureAnalyzer
sections.content:
**The contract**
- Extend `AbstractFailureAnalyzer<T>` where `T` is the exception type to handle
- Return a `FailureAnalysis` with description, action, and the cause
- Spring's exception chain walking finds the cause type anywhere in the chain (not just the immediate cause)

**Implementation example**

```java
public class MissingApiKeyAnalyzer
        extends AbstractFailureAnalyzer<ApiKeyMissingException> {

    @Override
    protected FailureAnalysis analyze(Throwable rootFailure,
                                       ApiKeyMissingException cause) {
        return new FailureAnalysis(
            "Required API key 'payment.gateway.key' is not configured.",
            "Set PAYMENT_GATEWAY_KEY environment variable or add " +
            "payment.gateway.key to application.yml",
            cause
        );
    }
}
```

**Registration (Boot 3.x)**
- Create `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer`
- One fully-qualified class name per line
- Pre-2.7: register in `META-INF/spring.factories` under the `FailureAnalyzer` key

**Why this matters in production**
- Instead of a stack trace, developers see a formatted message with the exact property name and how to set it
- New team members get actionable error messages instead of debugging stack traces
- Especially valuable for shared platform starters where consumers can't read the library code

**The `rootFailure` vs `cause` parameters**
- `rootFailure` — the outermost exception (usually `BeanCreationException`)
- `cause` — the specific typed exception you declared as `T`
- Spring's machinery walks the exception chain so your analyzer fires even when wrapped several layers deep

sections.title: Application Listeners and EnvironmentPostProcessor
Banners and ApplicationContextInitializer
Startup Customization Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When `FailureAnalyzer` helps:**
- Common deployment failures (missing env vars, port conflicts, schema mismatch)
- Onboarding — actionable messages instead of stack traces
- Shared platform starters where consumers can't read library code

**When `EnvironmentPostProcessor` helps:**
- Secret injection from Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager
- Custom property source formats not supported by Boot natively
- Property values that must be available before any bean reads the environment

**Watch for:**
- Confusing `ApplicationListener` (pre-context) with `@EventListener` (post-context)
- `EnvironmentPostProcessor` that throws — propagates as a startup failure with no context
- Custom banners with secrets or deployment metadata that shouldn't appear in logs
- `FailureAnalyzer` that swallows the underlying exception — always pass `cause` to the analysis
- Long-running listeners delaying startup measurably
- `spring.factories` typos — silently no-op (no class loaded)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`ApplicationListener` vs `@EventListener`** — `ApplicationListener<E>` registered as a bean fires for events after the `ApplicationContext` is created; `SpringApplication.addListeners()` or `spring.factories` registration fires for events before the context exists (e.g., `ApplicationStartingEvent`).
- **`ApplicationContextInitializer` runs before bean refresh** — modify the `ConfigurableApplicationContext` before any beans are created; used for adding property sources, setting active profiles programmatically.
- **`EnvironmentPostProcessor` adds properties before the context starts** — loads external secrets, vault config, or custom property formats before `@Value` injection; registered in `spring.factories`.
- **`FailureAnalyzer` produces human-readable startup failure messages** — implement to replace cryptic stack traces with actionable diagnostics; Spring Boot ships 20+ built-in analyzers for common errors.
- **`Banner` customization is cosmetic but has log value** — `banner.txt` placeholders display app name and version on every startup; `spring.main.banner-mode=off` for CI.
- **Boot 3.x registration files** — `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer` (one class per line); `spring.factories` still works for backward compatibility.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot's startup pipeline has extension points at every phase — before the context exists, before beans are created, after everything is ready, and when startup fails. Knowing which hook fires when determines which customization goes where.

**Before the context is created**
- `SpringApplication.addListeners(new MyListener())` registers listeners that fire for early events like `ApplicationStartingEvent` and `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent`
- `EnvironmentPostProcessor` — add property sources from external systems (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) before `@Value` injection evaluates them
- `ApplicationContextInitializer` — set active profiles, add property sources, or modify the context before beans are registered

**After the context is ready**
- `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)` — fires when the application is fully started; the same timing as `CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner`
- `@EventListener(ApplicationStartedEvent.class)` — fires after context refresh but before runners

**When startup fails**
- `FailureAnalyzer` — implement this interface to produce a human-readable message explaining a startup failure; Spring Boot ships analyzers for port-in-use, missing beans, and failed conditions
- Your analyzer catches a specific exception type and returns an explanation with a suggested action — replace stack traces with actionable diagnostics for your team
- Register in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer` (Boot 3.x) or `spring.factories` (older)

**Banner**
- Cosmetic but has operational value — identifies the app name and version in aggregated logs
- Disable with `spring.main.banner-mode=off` if CI logs need to stay clean

In an interview, the strong answer is: **`FailureAnalyzer` for actionable error messages, `EnvironmentPostProcessor` for early property injection, listeners via `spring.factories` for pre-context events — three hooks for three different timing requirements**.

But the startup sequence has three customization points that solve real problems: banner customization for identifying which version is running in logs, application listeners for reacting to lifecycle events before the ApplicationContext exists, and FailureAnalyzer for turning cryptic startup exceptions into human-readable messages.
